extracted.intended_audience: writers and literary readers (poets, essayists, critics interested in originality, pastoral verse, and moral writing)
extracted.subtask_short: writing originality in prose and pastoral
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for producing and evaluating original moral prose and pastoral poetry — covers what counts as plagiarism, modes to achieve originality, use of human passions and contemporary manners, and how to judge innovators ('projectors').

rubrics_metrics.name: Naturalness and diversity in pastoral poetry
rubrics_metrics.description: Preference for poems that are 'equally natural and more diversified' — natural feeling combined with variation of circumstances is prized; the complaint of a shepherd at sight of another's prosperity is a perennial, legitimate subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: the first pastoral is preferred because it is 'equally natural and more diversified.' A strong pastoral should avoid artifice, present believable emotion (e.g., jealousy at another's ease), and vary circumstances to sustain interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pastoral imagery and sensory detail
rubrics_metrics.description: Pastoral description should combine the typical images of rural pleasure (cooling fountains, flow'ry meads, woods, sacred springs, bees, pruner's song, cooing doves, turtles) to create a composite picture of rural happiness: 'The description of Virgil's happiness in his little farm, combines almost all the images of rural pleasure.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use varied sensory images and familiar rural motifs in combination to evoke tranquility and felicity; such accumulated details are the mark of effective pastoral writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authenticity: real events over artful fiction
rubrics_metrics.description: True events produce stronger feeling than the most artful fiction: 'we can always feel more than we can imagine, and that the most artful fiction must give way to truth.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When possible, ground poems and essays in real incidents or authentic feeling; realism and genuine experience often outperform contrived invention in producing emotional effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plagiarism criterion: consider subject and independent coincidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Similarity of sentiment does not by itself prove plagiarism: 'A coincidence of sentiment may easily happen without any communication... before an author be charged with plagiarism... the subject on which he treats should be carefully considered.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not accuse similarity as plagiarism just because works resemble one another — especially in history, science, or morality where the subject imposes similar statements. Establish communication or unmistakable copying before charging plagiarism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality via choice of mode and style
rubrics_metrics.description: A moralist (or writer) may be original by varying form and method: 'he may familiarize his system by dialogues..., or subtilize it into a series of syllogistick arguments: he may enforce his doctrine by seriousness and solemnity, or enliven it by sprightliness and gaiety: he may deliver his sentiments in naked precepts, or illustrate them by historical examples: ... continued discourse, or ... short strictures, and unconnected essays.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choosing an uncommon or well-executed mode (dialogue, argument, brevity, vivacity, example-based exposition, etc.) can confer originality even on familiar subject matter. Cultivate the specific form that suits your gifts and intended readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adaptation to changing fashions and social modes
rubrics_metrics.description: Writers should 'observe the alterations which time is always making in the modes of life, that they may gratify every generation with a picture of themselves.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To attract contemporaries, reflect current customs, manners, and fashions (e.g., changing courtship rituals, new social ambitions, evolving vices). Sensitivity to what is recently practiced or prized makes familiar themes feel new.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combine limited passions with circumstances for variety
rubrics_metrics.description: Although the passions themselves are few, their combinations and external modifications yield infinite variety: 'The passions of the mind... are very few; but those few agitated and combined, as external causes shall happen to operate... make such frequent alterations on the surface of life.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create novelty by recombining basic human passions (love, hatred, ambition, avarice, idleness) with fresh situations, prevailing opinions, and accidental caprices to produce distinctive characters and plots.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of multiple works on the same topic
rubrics_metrics.description: Multiple books on the same subject are useful because different authors offer different clarity, method, embellishment or simplicity: 'We do not wonder, that historians... agree in their narration; or that authors, delivering the elements of science, advance the same theorems... yet it is not wholly without use to mankind, that books are multiplied.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not dismiss derivative-seeming works outright: evaluate them by style, method, clarity, and suitability to particular readers — different approaches serve different audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't judge actions solely by outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: It is common but unjust to judge people's actions only by success or failure: 'It has always been the practice of mankind, to judge of actions by the event... they who attain their wishes, never want celebrators... they that miscarry, are quickly discovered to have been defective.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing historical actors, innovators, or literary projects, separate the moral/technical quality of the attempt from its ultimate fortune. Avoid retroactive assignment of praise or blame purely based on outcome.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attitude toward projectors: encourage rather than dismiss novelty
rubrics_metrics.description: Many new undertakings are persecuted simply for being new; yet 'They who find themselves inclined to censure new undertakings, only because they are new, should consider, that the folly of projection is very seldom the folly of a fool... it proceeds often from the consciousness of uncommon powers.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating proposals and innovators, weigh their intentions, knowledge, and possible contribution rather than dismissing them for novelty. Recognize that even unsuccessful projects may advance knowledge or yield useful by-products.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typical traits and faults of projectors
rubrics_metrics.description: Projectors commonly unite 'extent of knowledge and greatness of design' and often fail by 'attempting things beyond their power... aspiring to performances to which, perhaps, nature has not proportioned the force of man.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect that ambitious innovators may overreach; evaluate them by the scope of their aim, intellectual capacity, and whether their failures nonetheless produce useful discoveries. Distinguish rashness from imaginative enterprise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral writing may legitimately resemble prior works
rubrics_metrics.description: Because right and wrong are immutable, moralists teaching the same truths will naturally resemble one another: 'The same indulgence is to be shown to the writers of morality: right and wrong are immutable; and those, therefore, who teach us to distinguish them, if they all teach us right, must agree with one another.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not penalize moral writing for reiterating timeless principles; instead judge moralists on clarity, method, and ability to address contemporary manners and needs.
